questions.title: Transfer Impedance Z12
questions.stem: In the circuit shown below, find the Z-parameter Z₁₂.
questions.quick: GPSC revised the final answer to option C. For Z-parameters, Z12 = V1/I2 with I1 = 0. With port 1 open, no current flows through the 10 Ω left series arm, so the voltage at port 1 equals the junction voltage produced by I2 through the 5 Ω shunt branch. Hence Z12 = 5 Ω.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The Z-parameter definition is crucial. For a two-port network,
V1 = Z11 I1 + Z12 I2 and V2 = Z21 I1 + Z22 I2.
To determine Z12, set I1 = 0, which means port 1 is open-circuited. Because the left 10 Ω branch terminates at an open port, it carries zero current and therefore has zero voltage drop. Current I2 entering port 2 flows through the 20 Ω series resistor to the central node and then through the 5 Ω shunt resistor to the common return. The central-node voltage is 5I2, and the open-circuit port-1 voltage is the same node voltage. Therefore V1/I2 = 5 Ω. This is why the final GPSC key changed the provisional choice.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

For Z12: open port 1 (I1=0), inject current at port 2, then find V1/I2.

**Important Exam Point**

Apply the Z-parameter test condition before combining resistors.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from B to C.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Network Theory → Two-Port Networks → Z Parameters .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

For Z12: open port 1 (I1=0), inject current at port 2, then find V1/I2.

### Common Mistake

The 10 Ω and 20 Ω series resistors are not both in the transfer path under the I1=0 condition.

### Exam Tip

Apply the Z-parameter test condition before combining resistors.

questions.title: Interaction of Stator and Rotor Fields
questions.stem: Electromagnetic torque in rotating electrical machinery is present when ________
options: Both stator and rotor windings carry current
questions.quick: In a conventional doubly excited rotating machine, electromagnetic torque results from interaction between stator and rotor magnetic fields; hence both windings must be excited and carry current for this torque-production mechanism.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Electromagnetic torque is produced when two magnetic fields have a tendency to align. In a conventional machine with both stator and rotor windings, stator current produces one field and rotor current produces the other. Their interaction creates tangential force and torque. The broader energy-conversion principle also includes reluctance torque, where a wound rotor current may not be required, but the question is framed around the standard doubly excited machine model represented by the given options.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Torque needs interacting fields, not merely a uniform air gap.

**Important Exam Point**

Identify whether the question refers to doubly excited torque or reluctance torque.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Electromechanical Energy Conversion → Torque Production .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Torque needs interacting fields, not merely a uniform air gap.

### Common Mistake

Overgeneralizing the statement to every machine type can cause confusion; switched-reluctance machines are a special case.

### Exam Tip

Identify whether the question refers to doubly excited torque or reluctance torque.

questions.title: Field Test
questions.stem: _________ test is used for determining the efficiency of a traction motor.
questions.quick: The field test is a regenerative/back-to-back test suited to DC series machines, including traction motors, and allows efficiency to be determined under load conditions without wasting full output power.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Traction motors are commonly DC series motors (in the classical syllabus), and ordinary no-load methods are unsuitable because a series motor must not be run at no load. The field test uses two similar mechanically coupled series machines, one operating as a motor and the other as a generator, so power circulates between them and the supply provides mainly the losses. From measured input and losses, efficiency can be determined at substantial load. Hopkinson's test is classically used for shunt machines, while Swinburne's is an indirect no-load test mainly for shunt/compound machines.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Series traction motor → think field test/regenerative loading.

**Important Exam Point**

Match the test method to the DC motor connection type.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → DC Motors → Testing of DC Series Motors .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Series traction motor → think field test/regenerative loading.

### Common Mistake

Do not select Swinburne's test for a series traction motor; no-load operation of a series motor is unsafe.

### Exam Tip

Match the test method to the DC motor connection type.

questions.title: Compensating Winding
questions.stem: A 400-V, 1000-A, lap wound DC machine has 10 poles, 860 armature conductors. The number of conductors in the pole face to give full compensation if pole face covers 70% of pole span is
questions.quick: For full compensation, the compensating ampere-turns under a pole face must cancel the armature ampere-turns in that region. Using the lap-wound armature data and 70% pole-arc coverage gives the keyed requirement of 3010 ampere-conductors/ampere-turn equivalent under the pole face.
formula: Armature AT/pole = Z Ia /(2 A P)
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

In a lap-wound DC machine the number of parallel armature paths A equals the number of poles P. Armature ampere-turns per pole are proportional to ZIa/(2AP). Only the portion of armature reaction under the pole face must be neutralized by the compensating winding, so the pole-arc/pole-pitch ratio multiplies the result. With Z=860, Ia=1000 A, A=P=10 and pole arc ratio 0.7:
AT/pole = 860×1000/(2×10×10) = 4300 AT/pole.
Compensating requirement under the pole face = 0.7×4300 = 3010 AT/pole. The wording says 'number of conductors', but the numerical option corresponds to the compensating ampere-turn requirement.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Compensating winding cancels armature reaction only under the pole arc.

**Important Exam Point**

Use A=P for lap winding before substituting.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → DC Machines → Armature Reaction .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Compensating winding cancels armature reaction only under the pole arc.

### Common Mistake

The option value is an ampere-turn figure; do not silently drop the armature current from the calculation.

### Exam Tip

Use A=P for lap winding before substituting.

questions.title: Effect of Large Air Gap
questions.stem: These days alternators are designed to have larger air gaps for __________.
questions.quick: GPSC's final key accepts 'All of the mentioned'. A larger air gap reduces synchronous reactance and armature-reaction sensitivity, which improves stability/parallel operation; appropriate air-gap design also helps achieve a smoother magnetic-field distribution.
formula: Larger air gap → magnetic reluctance ↑ → Xs generally ↓
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Modern alternator air-gap design is a compromise involving stability, waveform, excitation requirement and mechanical construction. A relatively larger air gap increases magnetic reluctance, so more field ampere-turns are needed, but it reduces armature-reaction effect and synchronous reactance. Lower Xs raises the steady-state power-angle stability limit Pmax≈3VE/Xs and makes parallel operation more stable. Pole shaping and air-gap distribution are also used to improve the sinusoidal nature of the air-gap flux/mmf. Hence the final key was revised from a single item to 'all of the mentioned'.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Large air gap costs excitation but improves stability.

**Important Exam Point**

Think in terms of synchronous reactance and power-angle limit.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from A to D.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Synchronous Machines → Alternator Design .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Large air gap costs excitation but improves stability.

### Common Mistake

Do not assume a larger air gap is universally 'better'; it increases required field ampere-turns.

### Exam Tip

Think in terms of synchronous reactance and power-angle limit.

questions.title: Relative Speed of Air-Gap Field
questions.stem: A synchronous machine has field winding on stator and polyphase armature winding on rotor. At steady state, which of the following is not true for its air gap field?
options: Rotating at double the speed Ns w.r.t. rotor
Rotating in direction opposite to rotor
questions.quick: The final GPSC answer is B. A field winding placed on the stator produces an air-gap field stationary with respect to the stator. A rotor moving at synchronous speed sees that stationary field moving backward at Ns, not at 2Ns.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Take the stator as the stationary reference. The DC field winding on the stator establishes a stationary spatial field. The rotor carrying the polyphase armature rotates mechanically at synchronous speed Ns. Relative to the rotor, a field that is stationary in the stator frame appears to move at Ns in the opposite direction. Therefore 'rotating at double the speed Ns with respect to the rotor' is the statement that is not true. The other statements describe the same relative-motion picture in different frames.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Always subtract angular speeds when changing reference frames.

**Important Exam Point**

Write both field and rotor speeds in the same reference frame before judging relative direction.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from D to B.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Synchronous Machines → Rotating Magnetic Fields .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Always subtract angular speeds when changing reference frames.

### Common Mistake

Adding speeds instead of subtracting them is what produces the incorrect 2Ns conclusion.

### Exam Tip

Write both field and rotor speeds in the same reference frame before judging relative direction.

questions.title: Real Power Control
questions.stem: The active power delivered by an alternator will _______ when the prime mover input is increased for the alternator connected to infinite bus bar.
options: no relation exists between the power and prime mover droop characteristic
questions.quick: For an alternator connected to an infinite bus, bus voltage and frequency are fixed. Increasing prime-mover mechanical input increases torque angle δ and therefore increases the active power delivered to the bus.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

An infinite bus is so large that one generator cannot appreciably change its voltage or frequency. Once synchronized, mechanical input from the prime mover mainly controls real power, while field excitation mainly controls reactive power/power factor. Increasing turbine or engine input accelerates the rotor momentarily, increasing power angle δ until the electromagnetic power rises to a new balance. Thus active power output increases.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Prime mover controls MW; excitation controls MVAr.

**Important Exam Point**

Keep infinite-bus voltage and frequency fixed in your reasoning.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Synchronous Machines → Alternator on Infinite Bus .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Prime mover controls MW; excitation controls MVAr.

### Common Mistake

Do not expect frequency to rise appreciably when a single generator is tied to an infinite bus.

### Exam Tip

Keep infinite-bus voltage and frequency fixed in your reasoning.

questions.title: Transformer Analogy
questions.stem: An induction motor can be said analogous to _________
questions.quick: An induction motor is essentially a transformer with a rotating, short-circuited secondary. The stator acts like the primary and the rotor like the secondary, with power crossing the air gap electromagnetically.
formula: Equivalent rotor resistance for power split:
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Both transformers and induction motors operate by mutual induction. The stator winding produces an alternating/rotating magnetic field that induces rotor emf and current, just as transformer primary flux induces secondary emf. At standstill the analogy is especially direct; during rotation, rotor frequency becomes sf rather than supply frequency and the mechanical output introduces the slip-dependent equivalent resistance R2'/s. This transformer analogy is the foundation of the induction-motor equivalent circuit.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Induction motor = rotating transformer.

**Important Exam Point**

Use the transformer equivalent circuit first, then introduce slip.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Induction Motors → Equivalent Circuit .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Induction motor = rotating transformer.

### Common Mistake

Do not equate an induction motor to a synchronous motor; its torque requires slip.

### Exam Tip

Use the transformer equivalent circuit first, then introduce slip.

questions.title: Test Connections
questions.stem: While conducting open circuit test and short circuit test on a transformer, status of low voltage and high voltage windings will be such that in ____________
options: OC test − h.v. open, SC test − l.v. short-circuited
OC test − l.v. open, SC test − h.v. short-circuited
OC test − l.v. open, SC test − l.v. short-circuited
OC test − h.v. open, SC test − h.v. short-circuited
questions.quick: In the usual transformer tests, the open-circuit test is performed by energizing the LV side and leaving the HV side open. The short-circuit test is usually performed by shorting the LV side and applying a reduced voltage to the HV side. This matches option A.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The OC test needs rated voltage but only a small no-load current. Supplying the LV winding is convenient and safer for instruments, while the HV winding is left open. The SC test needs only a small fraction of rated voltage but full-load current. The LV winding is commonly shorted and the reduced test voltage is applied to the HV winding so that the current on the HV side is smaller and easier to measure. The exact side chosen can be changed in practice, but the standard exam convention is the one stated in option A.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

OC: open HV. SC: short LV (standard laboratory convention).

**Important Exam Point**

Focus on why instruments are conveniently connected to the chosen side.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Transformers → OC and SC Tests .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

OC: open HV. SC: short LV (standard laboratory convention).

### Common Mistake

Do not confuse which side is energized with which side is open/shorted.

### Exam Tip

Focus on why instruments are conveniently connected to the chosen side.

questions.stem: A 2000/1000/500 three winding transformer is to be used as auto transformer with supply of 3000V. Two loads of 1050 kVA at 3500 V and other one at 180 kVA at 1000 V. The total kVA supplied will be
questions.quick: The two specified loads are 1050 kVA and 180 kVA. The total apparent power supplied to the loads is therefore 1050 + 180 = 1230 kVA, matching option A.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The question supplies two simultaneous load ratings connected to different voltage points of a three-winding transformer used in an autotransformer arrangement. When asked for total kVA supplied, apparent powers of the loads are added (assuming the ratings represent simultaneous delivered apparent power). The internal conductive/transformative kVA split is relevant to winding rating and copper economy, but it does not change the total external load kVA delivered.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

External total kVA = sum of simultaneous load kVA values.

Do not confuse autotransformer transformed kVA with total load kVA.

questions.title: Load Sharing and Power Factor
questions.stem: Two single phase transformers A and B are operating in parallel having different impedance and identical x/r ratio. Then __________
options: A has poorer pf than B
B has poorer pf than B
Both operate at same power factor
questions.quick: If two transformers have different impedance magnitudes but identical X/R ratios, their impedance angles are equal. They may share unequal magnitudes of load, but the load-current phase angles are the same, so both operate at the same power factor.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

For transformers in parallel with equal voltage ratios, circulating-current issues aside, load division is inversely proportional to their complex impedances. If ZA and ZB have the same X/R ratio, they have the same impedance angle. Multiplying the common load current by complex division changes magnitude according to |Z| but does not introduce a different phase angle between each transformer's current and the common terminal voltage. Hence both transformer currents have the same power factor, although their kVA sharing may be unequal.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Same X/R ratio ⇒ same impedance angle ⇒ same load-current power factor.

**Important Exam Point**

Separate load-sharing magnitude from power-factor angle.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electrical Machines → Transformers → Parallel Operation .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Same X/R ratio ⇒ same impedance angle ⇒ same load-current power factor.

### Common Mistake

Different percentage impedance does not automatically mean different power factor if impedance angles are identical.

### Exam Tip

Separate load-sharing magnitude from power-factor angle.

questions.title: Solenoidal Vector Field
questions.stem: A vector is said to be solenoidal when its
questions.quick: A solenoidal vector field is divergence-free: ∇·A = 0. Physically, it has no net source or sink within the region.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Divergence measures the local net outward flux density of a vector field. If divergence is zero everywhere in a region, the field is called solenoidal. Magnetic flux density B is a classic example because ∇·B=0 expresses the absence of magnetic monopoles. Curl is a different operator that measures local rotation and does not define solenoidality.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Solenoidal = divergence zero; irrotational = curl zero.

**Important Exam Point**

Pair the two vocabulary words with the correct vector operator.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Vector Calculus → Divergence .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Solenoidal = divergence zero; irrotational = curl zero.

### Common Mistake

Do not confuse solenoidal with curl-free; a field can be divergence-free and still have nonzero curl.

### Exam Tip

Pair the two vocabulary words with the correct vector operator.

questions.title: Volume Integration
questions.stem: Find the power, given energy E = 2J and current density J = x2 varies from x = 0 and x = 1.
questions.quick: Using the given constant electric-field magnitude 2 and current density J = x² over x=0 to 1, power is the integral of E·J: ∫₀¹2x²dx = 2/3.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Electromagnetic power density delivered to charges is p_v = E·J in W/m³. Interpreting the problem as a one-dimensional unit cross-section with E=2 and J=x², total power is obtained by integrating the power density along x from 0 to 1. The integral of x² is x³/3, so the result is 2/3 in the implied power units. The key is not to integrate J alone; the electric field factor must multiply it.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Power density in a conductor/field region = E·J.

**Important Exam Point**

Check whether the problem implies unit area/volume when geometry is omitted.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Energy and Power → Field Power Density .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Power density in a conductor/field region = E·J.

### Common Mistake

Calling the given 2 'energy' instead of field quantity makes the wording awkward; use the dimensional relationship intended by the options.

Check whether the problem implies unit area/volume when geometry is omitted.

questions.title: Irrotational/Curl-Free Field
questions.stem: Find the value of Stoke’s theorem for A = x i + y j + z k. The state of the function will be
questions.quick: For A = x i + y j + z k, each component depends only on its corresponding coordinate. All cross-partial derivatives in ∇×A are zero, so the field is curl-free (irrotational).
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Compute curl directly:
∇×A = (∂Az/∂y - ∂Ay/∂z)i + (∂Ax/∂z - ∂Az/∂x)j + (∂Ay/∂x - ∂Ax/∂y)k.
For Ax=x, Ay=y, Az=z, every cross derivative is zero. Hence curl A = 0. In fact A = ∇[(x²+y²+z²)/2], so it is a conservative gradient field. Stokes' theorem is consistent with this: the circulation around any closed contour in a simply connected region is zero.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Components x,y,z with no cross-coordinate dependence usually make curl checks very quick.

**Important Exam Point**

Write the determinant/cross-derivative form once and inspect which derivatives vanish.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Vector Calculus → Curl .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Components x,y,z with no cross-coordinate dependence usually make curl checks very quick.

### Common Mistake

Divergence is 3 here, so the field is not solenoidal; curl-free does not mean divergence-free.

### Exam Tip

Write the determinant/cross-derivative form once and inspect which derivatives vanish.

questions.title: Flux Through a Closed Sphere
questions.stem: Evaluate the surface integral ∫∫ (3x i + 2y j). dS, where S is the sphere given by x² + y² + z² = 9.
questions.quick: Use Gauss' divergence theorem. For F = 3x i + 2y j, ∇·F = 3 + 2 = 5. The sphere x²+y²+z²=9 has radius 3 and volume 36π, so the outward flux is 5×36π = 180π.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

A closed-surface flux integral is usually faster through the divergence theorem than by parametrizing the sphere. The divergence of 3x i + 2y j is constant:
∂(3x)/∂x + ∂(2y)/∂y + ∂(0)/∂z = 5.
The sphere radius is 3, so its volume is (4/3)π(3³)=36π. Integrating constant divergence 5 over that volume gives 180π. This is the net outward flux through the entire spherical surface.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Closed surface + simple divergence → use divergence theorem immediately.

**Important Exam Point**

Confirm the surface is closed before replacing a surface integral with a volume integral.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Vector Calculus → Divergence Theorem .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Closed surface + simple divergence → use divergence theorem immediately.

### Common Mistake

Using surface area 4πr² instead of sphere volume is the common mistake in divergence-theorem questions.

### Exam Tip

Confirm the surface is closed before replacing a surface integral with a volume integral.

questions.title: Electric Flux Density of Charged Cylinder
questions.stem: Three charged cylindrical sheets are present in three spaces with σ = 5 at R = 2m, σ = − 2 at R = 4m and σ = − 3 at R = 5m. Find the flux density at R = 3m.
questions.quick: At r = 3 m only the cylindrical sheet at r = 2 m is enclosed; the sheets at 4 m and 5 m lie outside. Gauss' law gives D(r) = σa/r = 5×2/3 = 10/3 in the radial direction.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Choose a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius r=3 m and length L. The enclosed charge is σ(2πaL) from the sheet at a=2 m. The outer charged sheets do not contribute to enclosed charge at this Gaussian radius. By symmetry D is radial and constant on the cylindrical Gaussian surface, so D(2πrL)=σ(2πaL), yielding D=σa/r=10/3. This is a direct application of Gauss' law for an infinite cylindrical sheet.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

For concentric sheets, include only charges with radius less than the observation radius.

**Important Exam Point**

List enclosed sheets before writing Gauss' law.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Gauss Law → Cylindrical Charge Distribution .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

For concentric sheets, include only charges with radius less than the observation radius.

### Common Mistake

Adding charges from the 4 m and 5 m sheets at r=3 m violates the enclosed-charge rule.

### Exam Tip

List enclosed sheets before writing Gauss' law.

questions.title: EMF from Time-Varying Flux
questions.stem: Calculate the emf when the flux is given by 3sin t + 5cos t.
questions.quick: Faraday's law gives e = -dΦ/dt. For Φ = 3 sin t + 5 cos t, dΦ/dt = 3 cos t - 5 sin t, so e = -3 cos t + 5 sin t.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The induced emf polarity is governed by Lenz's law, represented by the minus sign in Faraday's law. Differentiate each term of flux with respect to time, then apply the negative sign to the entire derivative. The derivative of sin t is cos t and of cos t is -sin t. Thus dΦ/dt = 3cos t - 5sin t and e = -3cos t + 5sin t.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Differentiate first, apply Lenz's minus sign last.

questions.title: Charge Conservation from Maxwell Equations
questions.stem: The continuity equation is a combination of which of the two laws?
questions.quick: The continuity equation follows by taking the divergence of the Ampère-Maxwell law and using Gauss' law. This yields ∇·J = -∂ρv/∂t.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Ampère-Maxwell law states ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t. Taking divergence of both sides gives zero on the left because divergence of a curl is always zero. On the right, ∇·J + ∂(∇·D)/∂t = 0. Gauss' law gives ∇·D = ρv. Substituting produces ∇·J + ∂ρv/∂t = 0, the differential continuity equation expressing conservation of charge. Thus the two field laws used are Ampère-Maxwell and Gauss.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Continuity equation = divergence of Ampère-Maxwell + Gauss law.

**Important Exam Point**

Remember the vector identity ∇·(∇×H)=0.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Maxwell Equations → Continuity Equation .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Continuity equation = divergence of Ampère-Maxwell + Gauss law.

### Common Mistake

Ohm's law is not required to derive charge continuity.

### Exam Tip

Remember the vector identity ∇·(∇×H)=0.

questions.title: Checksum Error Detection
questions.stem: Which of these error-detecting codes enables to find double errors in Digital Electronic devices?
questions.quick: Among the listed choices, checksum coding is the method intended to provide stronger error detection, including many multi-bit error patterns. A simple parity bit reliably detects an odd number of bit errors but can miss two-bit errors because parity may remain unchanged.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Error-detecting schemes differ in capability. Single parity adds only one redundant bit; flipping two bits can preserve the original parity, so double-error detection is not guaranteed. A checksum combines blocks of data and compares a computed check value at the receiver, giving broader error-detection capability than simple parity in the context of the given options.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

If the question contrasts parity with checksum for multiple errors, parity is the weaker choice.

**Important Exam Point**

Distinguish 'can detect some double errors' from 'guarantees detection of every double error'; the wording of coding questions matters.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Digital Electronics → Digital Codes → Error Detection .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

If the question contrasts parity with checksum for multiple errors, parity is the weaker choice.

### Common Mistake

Assuming a parity bit detects every two-bit error.

### Exam Tip

Distinguish 'can detect some double errors' from 'guarantees detection of every double error'; the wording of coding questions matters.

questions.title: Half Adder Sum
questions.stem: If A and B are the inputs of a half adder, then the sum is given by __________
questions.quick: A half adder adds two single-bit inputs. Its Sum output is 1 only when A and B are different, which is exactly the XOR truth table; the Carry output is A·B.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

For inputs 00, 01, 10, 11, the binary sums are 0, 1, 1, 10. Hence the Sum bit sequence is 0,1,1,0 = A ⊕ B, while the Carry is 0,0,0,1 = AB. This is one of the basic identities used to build a full adder.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Half adder: XOR for Sum, AND for Carry.

**Important Exam Point**

Memorize the pair together; exam distractors often swap Sum and Carry.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Digital Electronics → Combinational Logic → Adders .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Half adder: XOR for Sum, AND for Carry.

### Common Mistake

Selecting OR for Sum; OR fails for A=B=1 because the correct sum bit is 0 with carry 1.

### Exam Tip

Memorize the pair together; exam distractors often swap Sum and Carry.

questions.title: Conduction Current Density
questions.stem: Calculate the conduction current density when the resistivity of a material with an electric field of 5 units is 4.5 units.
questions.quick: Conduction current density is related to electric field by the point form of Ohm’s law: J = σE = E/ρ. With E = 5 and resistivity ρ = 4.5, the current density is 5/4.5 ≈ 1.11 in the corresponding current-density units.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Resistivity tells us how strongly a material opposes conduction. Conductivity is its reciprocal, σ = 1/ρ. Therefore a finite electric field produces a conduction current density J = σE. The correct numerical value follows directly from dividing the field intensity by resistivity; multiplying E by ρ would reverse the physical relationship.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Remember: resistivity in denominator, conductivity in numerator.

**Important Exam Point**

Do a dimensional/physical sense check: larger resistivity must reduce J for the same E.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Electromagnetic Fields → Conduction and Current Density → Point Form of Ohm's Law .

### Quick Trick

Remember: resistivity in denominator, conductivity in numerator.

### Common Mistake

Using J = ρE instead of J = E/ρ.

### Exam Tip

Do a dimensional/physical sense check: larger resistivity must reduce J for the same E.

questions.title: Logic Gate Fan-Out
questions.stem: When can one logic gate drive many other logic gates in Digital Electronics?
options: When its output impedance is low and the input impedance is low
When its output impedance is high and the input impedance is high
When its output impedance is high and the input impedance is low
When its output impedance is low and the input impedance is high
questions.quick: One logic output can drive many logic inputs when the driving gate has low output impedance and the receiving gates have high input impedance. This minimizes loading, so the output voltage remains within valid logic levels even when several inputs are connected.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Fan-out is limited by the current a logic output can source/sink compared with the input current demanded by each load. A low output impedance behaves like a stiff voltage source, while high input impedance means each receiving gate draws little current. That is the desirable combination for driving multiple gates.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Driver: low Zout; loads: high Zin.

**Important Exam Point**

Connect fan-out questions with loading and valid logic-level margins, not only resistance words.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Digital Electronics → Logic Families → Fan-Out and Loading .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Driver: low Zout; loads: high Zin.

### Common Mistake

Choosing high output impedance; it causes larger voltage drop under loading.

### Exam Tip

Connect fan-out questions with loading and valid logic-level margins, not only resistance words.

questions.stem: A 4-bit ripple counter consists of flip-flops, where each have a propagation delay from clock to Q output of 15 ns. For the counter to recycle from 1111 to 0000, it takes a total of ________

### Concept & Reasoning

Unlike a synchronous counter, a ripple counter does not switch every flip-flop from a common clock edge. One stage's output triggers the next, so delays accumulate. The 1111→0000 recycle can require the change to ripple through all four stages, giving the worst-case propagation delay.

Ripple counter worst-case delay = number of stages × delay per stage.

**Important Exam Point**

This cumulative delay limits the maximum reliable clock frequency.

Ripple counter worst-case delay = number of stages × delay per stage.

This cumulative delay limits the maximum reliable clock frequency.

questions.title: Parallel-Load Shift Register
questions.stem: A 4-bit shift register that receives 4 bits of parallel data will shift to the ________ by ________ position for each clock pulse.
questions.quick: A 4-bit shift register loaded in parallel still shifts one bit position for each clock pulse once placed in shift mode. Under the convention used in the question, it shifts one position to the right per clock.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Parallel loading determines how the initial 4-bit word enters; it does not mean four positions shift at once. During serial shift operation, every active clock moves each stored bit to the adjacent stage by one position. Direction is set by the register configuration/control input.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Parallel load ≠ parallel shift.

**Important Exam Point**

Read the direction stated/assumed by the device before tracing bits.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Digital Electronics → Sequential Logic → Shift Registers .

questions.title: Maximum Load Current from Delta-Star Transformer
questions.stem: A step-down delta-star transformer, with per-phase turns ration of 5, is fed from a 3-phase, 1100 V, 50 Hz source. The secondary of this transformer through a 3-pulse type rectifier feeds a R load of 10 Ω. Find the maximum value of the load current (phase).
questions.quick: The primary is delta-connected, so its phase voltage is 1100 V. With a per-phase turns ratio of 5, the star-secondary phase voltage is 1100/5 = 220 V rms. The three-pulse rectifier's maximum load voltage is the phase-voltage peak, so I_max = √2×220/10 = √2×22 A.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Because the primary is delta, V1,phase = V1,line = 1100 V. The per-phase turns ratio N1/N2=5 gives V2,phase=220 V rms. A three-pulse midpoint rectifier connected to the star secondary uses the phase-to-neutral secondary voltages, whose peak is √2V2,phase. For a 10 Ω resistive load, the maximum instantaneous load current is therefore √2×22 A. This calculation is a good example of why line/phase voltage must be resolved before applying transformer ratio and rectifier relations.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Convert line/phase voltage before applying turns ratio.

**Important Exam Point**

Always write the delta/star line-to-phase relationships; this avoids √3 errors.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → Rectifiers → Three-Pulse Rectifier .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Convert line/phase voltage before applying turns ratio.

### Common Mistake

Using line voltage directly on the star-connected secondary without checking the phase relation.

### Exam Tip

Always write the delta/star line-to-phase relationships; this avoids √3 errors.

questions.title: Non-Circulating Current Dual Converter
questions.stem: In non-circulating current mode dual converters, the circulating current is avoided by
questions.quick: A non-circulating-current dual converter prevents the two converter bridges from conducting simultaneously. Only one converter is enabled at a time; an interlocking/dead-time scheme blocks the other, so there is no closed path for circulating current.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Dual converters provide reversible DC voltage/current using two controlled rectifier bridges. In circulating-current mode both bridges may operate simultaneously and a reactor limits the current caused by instantaneous voltage differences. In non-circulating mode, simultaneous conduction is deliberately prevented; the bridges are alternately enabled.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Reactor → circulating-current mode; one bridge at a time → non-circulating mode.

**Important Exam Point**

Look for interlocking/dead time in practical implementations.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → Converters → Dual Converters .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Reactor → circulating-current mode; one bridge at a time → non-circulating mode.

### Common Mistake

Selecting α1+α2=180° alone; that voltage relation does not by itself eliminate simultaneous-current paths.

### Exam Tip

Look for interlocking/dead time in practical implementations.

questions.title: Single-Pulse PWM Symmetry
questions.stem: In the single−pulse width modulation method, the output voltage waveform is symmetrical about ____________ in the negative half cycle.
questions.quick: For a single-pulse PWM waveform, the negative-half-cycle pulse is symmetrically located about 3π/2, just as the positive-half-cycle pulse is symmetric about π/2. This half-wave symmetry helps define the Fourier components.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

A full electrical cycle spans 0 to 2π. The center of the positive half-cycle is π/2 and the center of the negative half-cycle is 3π/2. A single pulse of controlled width is placed symmetrically about these centers, with opposite polarity in the negative half-cycle.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Centers of half cycles: π/2 and 3π/2.

**Important Exam Point**

Sketch one 0–2π cycle before answering PWM symmetry questions.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → Inverters → Pulse Width Modulation .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Centers of half cycles: π/2 and 3π/2.

### Common Mistake

Choosing π/2 for the negative half-cycle center.

### Exam Tip

Sketch one 0–2π cycle before answering PWM symmetry questions.

questions.title: Selective Harmonic Elimination in Single-Pulse PWM
questions.stem: In the case of a single−pulse width modulation with the pulse width = 2d, to eliminate the nth harmonic from the output voltage
questions.quick: For a single pulse of half-width d, the nth harmonic term contains sin(nd). To eliminate the nth harmonic, set sin(nd)=0; the non-trivial condition used in the options is nd = π.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Fourier analysis of the single-pulse waveform shows that the amplitude of an nth harmonic is proportional to sin(nd)/n (with additional symmetry restrictions on even/odd harmonics). Therefore harmonic elimination is achieved by choosing a pulse width such that the sine factor vanishes.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

See sin(nd) in harmonic coefficient → set nd to π for first non-zero root.

**Important Exam Point**

Check whether d is half pulse width; the question defines full pulse width as 2d.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → Inverters → Pulse Width Modulation .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

See sin(nd) in harmonic coefficient → set nd to π for first non-zero root.

### Common Mistake

Setting 2d=π irrespective of harmonic number.

### Exam Tip

Check whether d is half pulse width; the question defines full pulse width as 2d.

questions.title: Electric Heating Control
questions.stem: The AC voltage controllers are used in __________ applications.
questions.quick: AC voltage controllers vary the rms AC voltage supplied to a load without changing the supply frequency. A classic application is resistive electric heating, where delivered power is smoothly controlled by phase-angle or integral-cycle control.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

An AC voltage controller uses bidirectional semiconductor switches such as anti-parallel SCRs or a triac. By controlling the conduction interval, it changes the load rms voltage and therefore load power. Heating and lighting control are common applications; power generation/transmission are not the normal role of such controllers.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Variable AC rms voltage at same frequency → heating/lighting control.

**Important Exam Point**

For induction-motor applications, distinguish voltage control from variable-frequency drives.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → AC Voltage Controllers → Applications .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Variable AC rms voltage at same frequency → heating/lighting control.

### Common Mistake

Confusing an AC voltage controller with an inverter or frequency converter.

### Exam Tip

For induction-motor applications, distinguish voltage control from variable-frequency drives.

questions.title: N-Stage Sequence Controller Transformer Rating
questions.stem: In a N-stage sequence controller, each secondary is rated for __________
questions.quick: In an N-stage sequence controller, the supply voltage is divided across the staged secondary arrangement; each secondary is designed for a fraction of the total controlled voltage. The keyed relation is Vs/n per stage.
formula: Voltage per equal stage = Vs / n
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Sequence controllers use staged transformer secondaries/switching so that voltage can be built up in discrete steps. If Vs represents the total secondary voltage available over n equal stages, an equal-voltage stage carries Vs/n. This keeps each controlled section at a manageable voltage rating.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Equal n stages → divide total stage voltage by n.

**Important Exam Point**

Define whether Vs means total or per-secondary voltage before applying the formula.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → High Voltage Generation → Sequence Controllers .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Equal n stages → divide total stage voltage by n.

### Common Mistake

Multiplying by n when the total voltage is being shared among n equal stages.

### Exam Tip

Define whether Vs means total or per-secondary voltage before applying the formula.

questions.title: SCR RMS Current Rating with Safety Factor
questions.stem: A single−phase AC switch is used in between a 230 V source and load of 2 kW and 0.8 lagging power factor. Determine the rms current rating required by the SCR. Use the factor of safety = 2.
questions.quick: The load current is I = P/(V·pf) = 2000/(230×0.8) ≈ 10.87 A. With a safety factor of 2, the required SCR rms current rating is about 21.74 A.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

For a single-phase load, real power is P = VIcosφ. First calculate the actual rms load current from real power, supply voltage and power factor. A device rating must then include the stated safety margin; multiplying the operating current by 2 gives the minimum selected current rating.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Power → current first; safety factor last.

**Important Exam Point**

Use real power and power factor together; 2 kW is not 2 kVA.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → AC Controllers → Thyristor Ratings .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Power → current first; safety factor last.

### Common Mistake

Calculating 2000/230 and forgetting the 0.8 power factor.

### Exam Tip

Use real power and power factor together; 2 kW is not 2 kVA.

questions.title: Pole-to-Pole DC Transmission Voltage
questions.stem: Two six pulse converters used for bipolar HVDC transmission system are rated at 1000 MW, ± 200 kV. What is the DC transmission voltage?
questions.quick: A ±200 kV bipolar HVDC system has one pole at +200 kV and the other at −200 kV with respect to ground. Therefore the pole-to-pole transmission voltage is 200 − (−200) = 400 kV.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The ± notation gives each pole's voltage relative to earth/neutral. In a bipolar scheme the useful voltage between conductors is twice the pole-to-ground magnitude. The MW rating is not needed to calculate this voltage.

±V bipolar link → conductor-to-conductor voltage = 2V.

Separate pole voltage from pole-to-pole transmission voltage.

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → HVDC Transmission → Bipolar HVDC .

±V bipolar link → conductor-to-conductor voltage = 2V.

### Common Mistake

Reporting 200 kV because each individual pole is rated 200 kV to ground.

### Exam Tip

Separate pole voltage from pole-to-pole transmission voltage.

questions.stem: The single−phase mid-point type cycloconverter uses __________ number of SCRs.

Cycloconverters directly convert fixed-frequency AC to lower-frequency AC. Midpoint single-phase cycloconverter: 2 + 2 = 4 SCRs.

Midpoint single-phase cycloconverter: 2 + 2 = 4 SCRs.

questions.title: SMPS Input Ripple
questions.stem: Choose the incorrect statement.
options: SMPS is less sensitive to input voltage variations
SMPS is smaller as compared to rectifiers
SMPS is a source of radio interference
questions.quick: SMPS units are compact and relatively tolerant of input-voltage variation, but their switching action can inject high-frequency ripple/noise and electromagnetic interference. Therefore 'SMPS has low input ripple' is the incorrect statement among the given choices.
formula: Switching loss/EMI are controlled using high-frequency filters and layout.
SMPS size ∝ inverse of practical switching frequency for magnetics, broadly.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

A switched-mode supply operates semiconductor devices at high frequency, allowing smaller magnetic components and high efficiency. Regulation can tolerate a wide input range. The same fast switching edges, however, create conducted and radiated EMI, so input/output filters are important. The question asks for the incorrect characteristic, so the ripple/noise statement must be read carefully.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

SMPS advantages: compact, efficient, regulated; drawback: EMI/switching noise.

**Important Exam Point**

Watch the word 'incorrect' before selecting an attractive advantage.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power Electronics → Switched Mode Power Supplies → SMPS Characteristics .

SMPS advantages: compact, efficient, regulated; drawback: EMI/switching noise.

Assuming switching automatically means low ripple everywhere without filtering.

questions.title: Aperiodic Signal Definition
questions.stem: When is x(t) said to be non-periodic signal?
options: If the equation x (t) = x (t + T) is satisfied for all values of T
If the equation x (t) = x (t + T) is satisfied for only one value of T
If the equation x (t) = x (t + T) is satisfied for no values of T
If the equation x (t) = x (t + T) is satisfied for only odd values of T
questions.quick: A continuous-time signal is periodic only if there exists at least one finite positive T such that x(t+T)=x(t) for all t. If no positive finite T satisfies that condition, the signal is non-periodic (aperiodic).
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The period condition must hold for every time t, but only one positive fundamental period needs to exist; integer multiples of it are also periods. Therefore the phrase 'no values of T' should be interpreted as no non-zero finite positive period.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Existence of one positive period is enough.

**Important Exam Point**

Do not mistake 'for all t' (time variable) with 'for all T' (candidate period).

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → Signal Classification → Periodic and Aperiodic Signals .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Existence of one positive period is enough.

### Common Mistake

Saying a periodic signal must satisfy the equation for every possible T.

### Exam Tip

Do not mistake 'for all t' (time variable) with 'for all T' (candidate period).

questions.title: Monotonic Function Test
questions.stem: Which of the following signals is monotonic?
questions.quick: A monotonic signal consistently moves in only one direction (non-increasing or non-decreasing) over its domain. Simplify each candidate and/or inspect its derivative; the keyed choice is the expression that reduces to a monotonic function.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The safest method is to differentiate candidate continuous-time functions. A derivative that keeps one sign indicates monotonic behavior. Periodic sine/cosine functions are generally not monotonic over the entire real line, and log(cos t) is not even defined for all t. The trigonometric identity sin²(2t)+cos²(2t)=1 can reduce one candidate to a simple linear function, which is monotonic.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Simplify identities before differentiating.

**Important Exam Point**

Monotonic does not mean 'always positive'; it means consistently non-increasing or non-decreasing.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → Signal Classification → Monotonic Signals .

### Quick Trick

Simplify identities before differentiating.

### Common Mistake

Rejecting a decreasing straight line because it is not increasing.

### Exam Tip

Monotonic does not mean 'always positive'; it means consistently non-increasing or non-decreasing.

questions.title: Parameter Condition for Bounded Output
questions.stem: For what values of k is the following system stable, y = (k² − 3k − 4)log(x) + sin(x)?
questions.quick: The term multiplying log(x) can become unbounded as x approaches 0⁺, so for the system to avoid that unbounded contribution its coefficient must be zero. Solve k²−3k−4=0, giving k=4 or k=−1.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Factor the parameter polynomial: k²−3k−4=(k−4)(k+1). If its coefficient is nonzero, log(x) can grow without bound for bounded positive inputs approaching zero, violating a BIBO-style bounded-output requirement. Setting the coefficient to zero leaves sin(x), which is bounded between −1 and 1.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Unbounded function term? Force its coefficient to zero.

**Important Exam Point**

After cancelling log(x), confirm the remaining sin(x) term is bounded.

Unbounded function term? Force its coefficient to zero.

Solving the quadratic incorrectly or checking only positive k.

questions.title: Half-Power Frequencies of Series RLC
questions.stem: A 440 V, 50 Hz AC source supplies a series LCR circuit with a capacitor and a coil. If the coil has 100 mΩ resistance and 15 mH inductance, then at a resonance frequency of 50 Hz, the half power frequencies of the circuit are ______________
questions.quick: For a high-Q series RLC circuit, bandwidth is Δf = R/(2πL). With R=0.1 Ω and L=15 mH, Δf≈1.061 Hz. Half-power frequencies lie approximately symmetrically around 50 Hz, giving about 49.47 Hz and 50.53 Hz; the nearest option is 49.57 Hz and 50.53 Hz.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

At series resonance the impedance is minimum and current is maximum. The half-power points occur where |Z|=√2R. For a narrow bandwidth, f₂−f₁=R/(2πL), and f₁f₂=f₀² exactly. Using these relationships gives frequencies close to the listed pair. The 440 V value does not affect the half-power frequencies.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Series RLC bandwidth depends on R/L, not supply voltage.

**Important Exam Point**

For higher accuracy use f₁f₂=f₀² together with f₂−f₁=BW.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → RLC Circuits → Resonance .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Series RLC bandwidth depends on R/L, not supply voltage.

### Common Mistake

Using 440 V in the frequency calculation.

### Exam Tip

For higher accuracy use f₁f₂=f₀² together with f₂−f₁=BW.

questions.title: Complex Exponential Eigenfunction of LTI System
questions.stem: A signal e^(−at) sin (ωt) is the input to a real linear time invariant system. Given K and ∅ are constants, the output of the system will be of the form Ke^(−bt) sin (vt + ∅). The correct statement among the following is __________
options: b need not be equal to a but v must be equal to ω
v need not be equal to ω but b must be equal to a
b must be equal to a and v must be equal to ω
b need not be equal to a and v need not be equal to ω
questions.quick: A damped sinusoid is the imaginary part of a complex exponential e^{(-a+jω)t}. For an LTI system, a complex exponential is an eigenfunction: the system changes only its complex gain, not the exponential's pole. Therefore the output retains the same decay rate a and angular frequency ω; only magnitude and phase change.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Write the input as Im{e^{(-a+jω)t}}. If the system has transfer function H(s), the response to e^{st} is H(s)e^{st} whenever the eigenfunction condition applies. H(-a+jω) contributes a constant magnitude K and phase φ. Thus the output form is Ke^{-at}sin(ωt+φ), giving b=a and v=ω.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

LTI system changes amplitude/phase of an exponential mode, not its exponent.

**Important Exam Point**

Recognize damped sinusoids as conjugate complex exponentials.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from A to C.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → LTI Systems → Eigenfunctions .

### Quick Trick

LTI system changes amplitude/phase of an exponential mode, not its exponent.

### Common Mistake

Assuming the system can arbitrarily change frequency while remaining LTI under this eigenfunction setting.

### Exam Tip

questions.title: Square-Wave Harmonic Power Ratio
questions.stem: A periodic square wave is formed by rectangular pulses ranging from −1 to +1 and period = 2 units. The ratio of the power in the 7th harmonic to the power in the 5th harmonic for this waveform is equal to ____________
questions.quick: For an ideal symmetric square wave, only odd harmonics are present and the nth harmonic amplitude is proportional to 1/n. Harmonic power is proportional to amplitude squared, so P7/P5=(5/7)²≈0.51, nearest to 0.5.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The Fourier series of a bipolar 50% duty square wave contains odd terms 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7, …. If the load resistance is the same for every harmonic, power contributed by one sinusoidal harmonic is proportional to V_n². Thus the ratio is the square of the amplitude ratio.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Square-wave harmonic power falls as 1/n².

**Important Exam Point**

Use amplitude ∝1/n, but power ∝1/n².

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → Fourier Series → Harmonics .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Square-wave harmonic power falls as 1/n².

### Common Mistake

Using 5/7 directly as the power ratio instead of squaring it.

### Exam Tip

Use amplitude ∝1/n, but power ∝1/n².

questions.title: Dirichlet/Fourier Convergence at Discontinuities
questions.stem: When is Fourier convergence theorem applicable?
questions.quick: Fourier convergence results determine the limiting value to which a Fourier series (an infinite trigonometric series) converges. Under the standard convergence conditions, the series converges to the function at continuity points and to the midpoint of a finite jump at discontinuities. In the wording of this MCQ, the applicable purpose is the limit of an infinite series.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

A Fourier series is an infinite series representation of a periodic function. The convergence theorem states the value approached by its partial sums under Dirichlet-type conditions. At a point of continuity the series converges to f(t); at a jump it converges to [f(t⁻)+f(t⁺)]/2. Consequently the theorem is used to establish/evaluate the limiting behavior of an infinite Fourier series. 'Break point limits' is an important special result inside the theorem, but the official final key selects the broader 'infinite series limit' description.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

At a discontinuity, Fourier series lands at the midpoint of the jump.

**Important Exam Point**

Remember Gibbs oscillation near a jump does not change the convergence midpoint at the jump itself.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → Fourier Series → Convergence .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

At a discontinuity, Fourier series lands at the midpoint of the jump.

### Common Mistake

Thinking the series converges to only the left or right limit.

### Exam Tip

Remember Gibbs oscillation near a jump does not change the convergence midpoint at the jump itself.

questions.title: Crest Factor of Common Waveforms
questions.stem: Which of the following waves has the highest value of peak factor?
questions.quick: Peak factor (crest factor) is V_peak/V_rms. For a half-wave rectified sine, V_rms=V_m/2, so peak factor=2, which exceeds sine (√2), triangular (√3) and square (1).
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Compare waveforms using the same definition rather than intuition about shape. A waveform with a relatively small rms value for a given peak has a larger crest factor. The half-wave rectified sine spends half the cycle at zero, lowering its rms relative to its peak.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Memorize crest factors: square 1, sine 1.414, triangle 1.732, half-wave sine 2.

**Important Exam Point**

Use rms definitions over the full waveform period.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → Waveform Parameters → Peak Factor .

Memorize crest factors: square 1, sine 1.414, triangle 1.732, half-wave sine 2.

Confusing form factor with peak factor.

Use rms definitions over the full waveform period.

questions.title: RL Time Constant
questions.stem: Time constant of an inductive circuit
options: increases with the increase of inductance and the decrease of resistance
increases with the increase of inductance and the increase of resistance
increases with the decrease of inductance and the decrease of resistance
increases with the decrease of inductance and the increase of resistance
questions.quick: For an RL circuit the time constant is τ=L/R. It increases when inductance increases and when resistance decreases, because larger L resists current change while larger R dissipates energy faster.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

After a DC step, current in a simple series RL circuit approaches its final value exponentially with time constant L/R. Roughly 63.2% of the total current change occurs after one time constant and more than 99% after about five time constants.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

L upstairs, R downstairs.

**Important Exam Point**

Use the Thevenin resistance seen by the inductor for more general first-order networks.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → First-Order Circuits → RL Transients .

L upstairs, R downstairs.

### Common Mistake

Writing τ=R/L, which has units of inverse seconds rather than seconds.

### Exam Tip

Use the Thevenin resistance seen by the inductor for more general first-order networks.

questions.title: Impulse Response Tests
questions.stem: The impulse response of an LTI system which is continuous is H (t) = e−|t|. The system is ___________
questions.quick: h(t)=e^{-|t|} is nonzero for t<0, so the system is not causal. But ∫|h(t)|dt over all time is finite (=2), so the LTI system is BIBO stable. Therefore it is stable but not causal.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

For a continuous-time LTI system, causality requires h(t)=0 for t<0. BIBO stability requires absolute integrability. Here e^{-|t|} is symmetric and decays exponentially on both sides, making its absolute integral finite, but its negative-time portion violates causality.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Check causality and stability independently.

**Important Exam Point**

Two-sided decaying impulse responses are often stable but noncausal.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → LTI Systems → Causality and Stability .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Check causality and stability independently.

### Common Mistake

Assuming exponential decay automatically implies causality.

### Exam Tip

Two-sided decaying impulse responses are often stable but noncausal.

questions.title: Form Factor Equals Peak Factor
questions.stem: Form factor is equal to peak factor in the case of
questions.quick: For an ideal square wave, the magnitude is constant throughout each half-cycle. Therefore peak value = rms value = average rectified value, making both peak factor and form factor equal to 1. Hence the two factors are equal for a square wave.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Peak factor is V_peak/V_rms, while form factor is V_rms/V_avg(rectified). For a symmetrical square wave of amplitude V_m, the rms value is V_m and the average of the rectified waveform is also V_m. Thus both ratios are exactly 1. Other common waveforms have different rms, average and peak relationships, so their two factors are not equal.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Write both definitions before comparing waveform tables.

**Important Exam Point**

Never use signed full-cycle average for AC form factor because it would be zero for symmetrical AC.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Signals and Systems → Waveform Parameters → Form Factor .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Write both definitions before comparing waveform tables.

### Common Mistake

Assuming form factor and peak factor are the same definition.

### Exam Tip

Never use signed full-cycle average for AC form factor because it would be zero for symmetrical AC.

questions.title: Subtransient Reactance Components
questions.stem: Which of the following reactances is eliminated first in synchronous generator just after the symmetrical fault?
questions.quick: Immediately after a sudden symmetrical fault, damper-winding currents produce the strongest opposing transient flux and therefore the smallest subtransient reactance. The effect associated with the damper winding decays first as those induced currents die out rapidly.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

A synchronous generator fault current passes through subtransient, transient and steady-state stages. Damper circuits dominate the very early subtransient interval; field-winding transients persist longer. As damper current decays, the effective reactance rises from Xd'' to Xd' and finally Xd.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

First few cycles → damper winding → subtransient reactance.

**Important Exam Point**

Link time sequence: damper dies first, field transient next.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Fault Analysis → Synchronous Generator Reactances .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

First few cycles → damper winding → subtransient reactance.

### Common Mistake

Confusing 'eliminated first' with the physically smallest static leakage reactance.

### Exam Tip

Link time sequence: damper dies first, field transient next.

questions.title: Voltage Regulation at Leading Power Factor
questions.stem: A transmission line Z = (2 + j8) Ω has 10% of the voltage regulation with the lagging load of 0.8. If the load is 0.707 leading, then the V.R. is ________ (Assume the current is same in both cases)
questions.quick: For a short-line approximation, voltage regulation is proportional to I(R cosφ + X sinφ) for lagging current, while the reactive term changes sign for leading current. Using the given 10% lagging case to eliminate the common I/V factor gives a negative regulation for 0.707 leading, about −6.63%.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

With R=2 Ω and X=8 Ω, the lagging 0.8 power factor has sinφ=0.6. The proportional drop factor is 2(0.8)+8(0.6)=6.4. For 0.707 leading, cosφ≈sinφ≈0.707 and the factor is 2(0.707)−8(0.707)=−4.242. Holding current and receiving voltage constant, regulation scales by −4.242/6.4, so 10% becomes about −6.63%.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Leading pf flips the sign of the X sinφ term.

**Important Exam Point**

Use the given 10% case as a ratio; no absolute line voltage is required.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Transmission Lines → Voltage Regulation .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Leading pf flips the sign of the X sinφ term.

### Common Mistake

Forgetting the negative reactive-drop term at leading power factor.

### Exam Tip

Use the given 10% case as a ratio; no absolute line voltage is required.

questions.title: CT Ratio Matching for Star-Delta Transformer
questions.stem: A three−phase transformer having a line voltage ratio of 400/33000 V is connected in the star-delta. The CTs on the 400V side have a CT ratio of 1000/5. What must be the ratio of CTs on the 33000 side?
questions.quick: Transformer differential protection requires the CT secondary currents presented to the relay to compensate for the transformer ratio and phase-connection effects. Using the given 400/33 kV transformer and 1000/5 CT on the LV side, the matching HV-side CT ratio corresponds to the keyed 7/5 value.
formula: Then include √3 CT-connection compensation for differential balance.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

In transformer differential schemes, CT connections are normally opposite to the power-transformer winding connections to compensate the 30° phase shift. The current magnitude on each side is inversely proportional to line voltage for the same MVA, and the delta-connected CT group introduces a √3 factor. A rigorous calculation should write line currents and relay-side currents explicitly before choosing the CT ratio.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Protection CT matching = transformer current ratio + CT star/delta compensation.

**Important Exam Point**

Draw transformer winding and CT connections before calculating relay currents.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Protection → Differential Protection .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Protection CT matching = transformer current ratio + CT star/delta compensation.

### Common Mistake

Using only 82.5:1 transformer line-current ratio and ignoring CT connection compensation.

### Exam Tip

Draw transformer winding and CT connections before calculating relay currents.

questions.title: Neutral Earthing Resistance and Relay Setting
questions.stem: The neutral of the three phase 20 MVA, 11 kV alternator is earthed through a resistance of 5 ohms. The relay is set to operate when there is an out of balance current of 1.5 A. The CTs have a ratio of 100/5. What should be the minimum value of the earthing resistance to protect 90% of winding?
questions.quick: First refer the relay setting through the CT ratio: 100/5 = 20, so a 1.5 A relay pickup corresponds to 30 A primary residual current. Restricted-earth-fault sensitivity is then related to the voltage available at the minimum protected winding point and the neutral earthing resistance. The official final key gives 2.12 Ω for the stated 90% protection condition.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

This is a protection-setting problem where the relay secondary pickup must be converted to primary current before using generator phase voltage and the protected winding percentage. For 90% winding protection, the minimum fault location is close to the neutral, so only a fraction of the full phase emf drives the earth-fault current. The exact convention adopted by the source calculation yields the keyed minimum earthing-resistance value of 2.12 Ω. In practice, restricted-earth-fault design also considers CT matching, stabilizing requirements and the neutral grounding method; the exam calculation should not be generalized without those assumptions.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Always refer relay current to primary before using system voltage.

**Important Exam Point**

Restricted earth-fault percentage protection depends on the available neutral-fault current and winding fraction.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Protection → Restricted Earth Fault .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Always refer relay current to primary before using system voltage.

### Common Mistake

Using 1.5 A directly as generator-side fault current.

### Exam Tip

Restricted earth-fault percentage protection depends on the available neutral-fault current and winding fraction.

questions.title: Reactive Power Compensation of Single-Phase Motor
questions.stem: A single−phase motor is connected to 400V, 50Hz supply. The motor draws a current of 31.7A at a power factor 0.7 lag. The additional reactive power (in VAR) to be supplied by the capacitor bank will be ___________
questions.quick: The motor apparent power is S=VI=400×31.7=12.68 kVA. At pf=0.7, real power is 8.876 kW and reactive power is Q=S√(1−0.7²)≈9.06 kVAR. For full correction to unity power factor, the capacitor must supply approximately 9055 VAR, matching the final key.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Power factor 0.7 lag means the motor absorbs inductive reactive power. A shunt capacitor supplies equal leading VARs if the target is unity power factor. Compute either Q=P tanφ or Q=S sinφ. The problem does not state a different target power factor, so the final key implies complete compensation.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

For unity correction, capacitor kVAR = original inductive kVAR.

**Important Exam Point**

State the target power factor; here the final answer assumes unity.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from A to D.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Power Factor Correction → Capacitor Banks .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

For unity correction, capacitor kVAR = original inductive kVAR.

### Common Mistake

Calculating capacitor VAR as P(1−pf) instead of Ptanφ.

questions.title: Isolated Generator Frequency with Droop
questions.stem: An isolated generator is connected to a turbine with its continuous maximum power of 20 MW, 50 Hz. Generator is connected with two loads of 8 MW, each operates at 50 Hz. Generator has 5% droop characteristic. If an additional load of 6 MW is added, then frequency will be ___________
questions.quick: The two existing loads total 16 MW. Adding 6 MW raises demand to 22 MW, but the turbine can continuously supply only 20 MW, leaving a 2 MW deficit beyond its headroom. With 5% droop on a 50 Hz, 20 MW unit, the frequency-power slope is 0.125 Hz/MW; the exam's steady-state simplification therefore gives a 0.25 Hz drop to 49.75 Hz.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Five-percent droop corresponds to a 2.5 Hz frequency change for a 20 MW full-range power change, so the slope is 2.5/20=0.125 Hz/MW. The machine is initially supplying 8+8=16 MW and has only 4 MW continuous headroom to its 20 MW turbine limit. A 6 MW added demand exceeds that headroom by 2 MW. Applying the exam's droop/shortfall convention gives Δf=0.125×2=0.25 Hz and f≈49.75 Hz. In a real isolated system, a fully saturated prime mover requires load-frequency dependence or load shedding for a true steady-state balance; that practical nuance is not specified in the MCQ.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Convert % droop to Hz/MW first.

**Important Exam Point**

An isolated governor with droop does not restore frequency exactly to 50 Hz without secondary control.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from D to C.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Load Frequency Control → Governor Droop .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Convert % droop to Hz/MW first.

### Common Mistake

Applying 5% directly to the 2 MW load instead of to rated power/frequency.

### Exam Tip

An isolated governor with droop does not restore frequency exactly to 50 Hz without secondary control.

questions.title: Root-Locus Asymptote Angles
questions.stem: The characteristic equation of a control system is given by s(s + 4)(s² + 2s + s) + k(s + 1) = 0. What are the angles of the asymptotes for the root loci?
questions.quick: Root-locus asymptote angles depend only on the excess number of open-loop poles over zeros: θ_k=(2k+1)180°/(n−m). For the characteristic equation, the open-loop structure gives three asymptotes, so the angles are 60°, 180° and 300°.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Rewrite the characteristic equation in 1+KG(s)H(s)=0 form and count open-loop poles and finite zeros. If n−m=3, the three asymptotes are equally spaced by 120° and begin at 60°. Their centroid needs pole/zero locations, but the question asks only angles.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Three asymptotes → 60°, 180°, 300°.

**Important Exam Point**

Angles depend on n−m, not on the numerical value of K.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Control Systems → Root Locus → Asymptotes .

Three asymptotes → 60°, 180°, 300°.

### Common Mistake

Using 0°,120°,240°, which corresponds to even-multiple angles rather than odd-multiple root-locus asymptotes.

Angles depend on n−m, not on the numerical value of K.

questions.title: Critically Damped Step Response
questions.stem: The unit step response of a second order system is = 1 − e^(−5t) − 5t e^(−5t). Consider the following statements:**1.** The under damped natural frequency is 5 rad/s.**2.** The damping ratio is1.**3.** The impulse response is 25t e^(−5t).Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.quick: The response 1−e⁻⁵ᵗ−5te⁻⁵ᵗ is the standard unit-step response of a critically damped second-order system with repeated pole at −5. Hence ζ=1, and differentiating the step response gives impulse response h(t)=25te⁻⁵ᵗ. Statement 1 is false because there is no underdamped natural frequency.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

For a critically damped system G(s)=ω_n²/(s+ω_n)² with ζ=1. Its unit-step response is 1−e^{-ω_n t}(1+ω_n t). Comparing with the given expression gives ω_n=5 rad/s and ζ=1. The damped oscillation frequency ω_d=ω_n√(1−ζ²)=0, so calling 5 rad/s an 'underdamped natural frequency' is incorrect. The impulse response is the derivative of the unit-step response.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Spot (1+ω_nt)e^{-ω_nt} → critically damped repeated pole.

**Important Exam Point**

Impulse response = derivative of unit-step response for an LTI system.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

The official GPSC final answer key revised the provisional outcome for this question from D to B.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Control Systems → Second-Order Systems → Time Response .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Spot (1+ω_nt)e^{-ω_nt} → critically damped repeated pole.

### Common Mistake

Calling ω_n=5 an underdamped frequency when ζ=1.

### Exam Tip

Impulse response = derivative of unit-step response for an LTI system.

questions.title: Effect of PI Control
questions.stem: Assertion (A): A PI controller increases the order of the system by units but decreases the steady state error.Reason (R): A PI controller introduces a pole at either the origin or at a desired points on the negative real axis.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.quick: A PI controller adds an integrator pole at the origin and a finite zero, increasing system type and reducing/eliminating steady-state error for appropriate inputs. The assertion is therefore true. The reason is false because a PI controller's added pole is specifically at the origin; the finite negative-real-axis point is the controller zero, not an arbitrary added pole.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

The PI transfer function is K_p + K_i/s = K_p(s+K_i/K_p)/s. It introduces one pole at s=0 and one zero at s=−K_i/K_p. The integrator raises low-frequency gain and can improve steady-state accuracy, but it also changes transient/stability characteristics. Reading pole versus zero correctly is the key to the assertion-reason pair.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

PI = pole at origin + finite zero.

**Important Exam Point**

Separate the roles of the integrator pole and controller zero.

**Editorial / Answer-Key Note**

questions.title: Sequence Voltages for Fault Types
questions.stem: If all the sequence voltages at the fault point in a power system are equal, then fault is __________
questions.quick: In a line-to-line-to-ground (LLG) fault, positive-, negative- and zero-sequence networks are all involved and their sequence voltages at the fault point are equal because the three sequence networks meet at a common fault-point voltage.
questions.detailed:
### Concept & Reasoning

Fault type determines how sequence networks interconnect. A three-phase balanced fault uses only the positive-sequence network. A line-to-line fault uses positive and negative sequences without zero sequence. A single line-to-ground fault places the three sequence networks in series, producing equal sequence currents. For an LLG fault, the sequence networks have a parallel-type connection at the fault point, making the sequence voltages equal.

### How to Solve It in the Exam

Equal sequence voltages → think LLG parallel sequence-network connection.

**Important Exam Point**

Memorize network interconnections, not just fault names.

### Related Revision Path

This question sits in the revision path Power System → Fault Analysis → Symmetrical Components .
questions.extra:
### Quick Trick

Equal sequence voltages → think LLG parallel sequence-network connection.

### Common Mistake

Confusing equal sequence currents of an LG fault with equal sequence voltages of an LLG fault.

### Exam Tip

Memorize network interconnections, not just fault names.
